plan.why: Highest-momentum radar item (92) in our strongest Short lane. Fast-moving news belongs in a Short rather than the long-form, and the lab results add a fact we haven't published. | fact-check: Confirmed: CBS News published on Oct 21, 2026 ('We bought and tested what was sold as an experimental weight loss drug…'). Three samples were tested: two bought online and one Brooklyn bodega vial ($90, labelled 'research use only, not for human consumption'). The analysis was by University of Iowa scientist Jason Galpin. Two fixes. (1) 'Matched only a basic reference standard' is stronger than the source. CBS says both online samples were 'consistent with a basic standard' Galpin created for retatrutide, which 'isn't the same as' Lilly's trial drug. The bodega vial had no peptide, only phenylacetic acid (a filler) and 13 bacteria colonies. The angle leaves out the bacteria, which is the key safety fact. (2) The Q1 2027 filing plan is not in the CBS piece. Credit it to Lilly's July 23, 2026 announcement (plans to submit to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027), from Lilly's own press release. Also check that the 'not approved by MHRA, Health Canada or TGA' claim is current as of Oct 2026, or limit the status line to the FDA. Lilly's statement in CBS mentions 'two deaths associated with black-market retatrutide'. If used, credit it to Lilly via CBS as Lilly's claim, without stating a cause. Don't name Reset Wellness, the gym or the bodega. No vial close-ups. This adds new facts on top of our earlier Bootleg Reta Short, so the variety guard is fine.

package.description:
CBS News lab-tested 3 products sold as retatrutide (Oct 21, 2026): the 2 bought online matched a basic standard, not Lilly's trial drug, and weren't reported tested for sterility or purity; a corner-store vial labelled "research use only" didn't appear to contain any peptide and had 13 colonies of bacteria.
Retatrutide is not FDA-approved and is still in clinical trials (CBS News, Oct 21, 2026). Lilly plans to file with the FDA in Q1 2027 (HCPLive, July 2026); a plan to file isn't approval. Ask a prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial.

factcheck.summary: I checked every factual claim against the two cited sources and all of them hold up. CBS News, Oct 21, 2026, bought and tested three samples sold as retatrutide: two online and one from a Brooklyn bodega in a vial labelled "Retatrutide". The two online samples were "consistent with a basic standard" made by University of Iowa research scientist Jason Galpin, "which isn't the same as the drug being studied in Eli Lilly's clinical trials." The article doesn't report testing the online samples for bacteria or sterility. The bodega vial was labelled "Research use only, not for human consumption." It "did not appear to even contain a peptide at all," Galpin called the compound in it (phenylacetic acid) "a filler," and a second Iowa scientist, Carl Ross, found 13 colonies of bacteria. CBS states retatrutide is "not FDA approved and still in clinical trials." HCPLive, Jul 23, 2026, reports Lilly plans to submit to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027. The script correctly says a plan to file isn't approval. A search found no sign Lilly has filed since. The safety framing is good: no sellers named, no buying instructions, it points to a prescriber, and it includes the "Not personal advice" and prescriber lines. The script is about 150 words. Three optional wording fixes are listed below.

issues.claim: HCPLive reported in July that Lilly plans to file with the FDA in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven.
issues.problem: The craft rules say every dated status needs a day, month and year. The narration says only "in July", while the on-screen attribution gives Jul 23, 2026.
issues.fix: HCPLive reported on July twenty-third, twenty twenty-six, that Lilly plans to file with the FDA in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven.

issues.problem: With the sound off, a viewer can't tell this is a company plan or who reported it. The stat label covers part of this, but the caption card should name the source too.
issues.fix: Not FDA-approved (CBS, Oct 21, 2026); Lilly plans FDA filing Q1 2027

issues.claim: Matched a basic standard, not shown safe
issues.problem: This doesn't name the drug, the source or the scope. A muted viewer could take "basic standard" to mean the real drug.
issues.fix: 2 online samples matched a basic lab standard, not Lilly's trial drug; not tested for sterility

notes: Caption spells out the number as 'THREE' instead of the numeral '3' used in the stat pill ('3 products lab-tested'), breaking the numerals-only rule.
Frame has no hero character, just floating test tubes and a microscope on an empty background — reads a bit sparse/dead.
Caption spells the year as 'TWENTY TWENTY-SIX' instead of '2026', contradicting the on-screen 'CBS News, Oct 21, 2026' pill.
Caption word order is garbled across the two cards ('ONLINE WERE CONSISTENT' then 'OF IOWA SCIENTIST MADE'), which doesn't parse as a sentence and won't be readable in under a second.
Caption card ends on a comma ('NOT FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION,'), which the style guide explicitly bans.
The building/'24H' icon plus the warning triangle added in the second frame crowd the top area next to the photo-frame icon, reading as cluttered rather than a clear focal point.
No on-screen headline — just a small 'Peptide?' tag, a molecule icon and a test tube on a plain purple background, which reads as sparse against the sparse-frame rule.
First caption card 'WHAT ONE CALLED' is a confusing, incomplete fragment that doesn't read as a sentence next to the '13' stat.
Caption ends on a comma ('...OCTOBER TWENTY-FIRST,') and spells out the date in words instead of using 'Oct 21' as shown in the source pill.
Caption card ends on a comma ('TWENTY TWENTY-SIX,') and spells the year out in words.
Caption spells the stat out as 'QUARTER OF TWENTY TWENTY-SEVEN' which doesn't match the on-screen stat pill 'Q1 2027' — a muted-viewer mismatch and a clear numerals violation.
